extracted.intended_audience: readers and makers of 19th-century political economy/policy pamphlets (higher and middle classes, gentry, policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: Persuasive political-economy pamphlet/polemic aimed at the higher and middle classes arguing reforms to agricultural policy, poor laws, and social duties; mixes moral argument with policy prescriptions. The page also contains a publisher's catalogue advertising editorial standards for a book series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landlords' objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Provided they are both faithful to their engagements, the objects of both will be: 1, the utmost produce that can be raised without injuring the estate; 2, with the least possible consumption of the produce on the estate itself; 3, at the lowest wages; and 4, with the substitution of machinery for human labour wherever the former will cost less and do the same work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement enumerates the practical aims that landlords and farmers pursue under the commercial system; presented as factual description of incentives driving agricultural management and labour policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common proposed remedies (criticised)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let measures be taken, that rents, taxes, and wages be lowered, and the markets raised! ... As the best remedies for this calamity, we propose that we should pay less to our landlords, less to our labourers, nothing to our clergyman, and either nothing or very little to the maintenance of the government and of the poor; but that we should sell at our former prices to the consumer!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author quotes and critiques a prevailing set of remedial proposals (reducing payments to various social actors while keeping consumer prices), using them as an anti-pattern to argue that such measures are unjust and socially harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of poor laws and perverse incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: In agricultural districts three-fourths of the poor rates are paid to healthy, robust, and (to sorrow and shame!) industrious, hard-working paupers in lieu of 'wages' (for men cannot at once work and starve): and therefore if there are twenty housekeepers in the parish, who are not holders of land, their contributions are so much bounty money to the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as evaluative criterion: the poor-law system creates perverse transfers (from non-landholding parishioners to landowners) and fosters dependency; cited consequences include dispossession of cow-pastures, increased poor rates, estate decay, and social destabilisation—evidence for judging poor-law reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agricultural management principle: consolidation and cheap labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Labour cheap, and estates let out in the fewest possible partitions — in other words, of large farms and low wages — each as indispensable to the other, and both conjointly as the only means of drawing capital to the land, by which alone the largest surplus is attainable for the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the argument in favour of large farms/low wages: a criterion for what proponents claim is efficient farm organisation. The author uses it to explain the rationale behind current practice and then to critique its social effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of an unchecked commercial spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessary consequences of the commercial spirit uncounteracted and unenlightened, wherever trade has been carried to a vast extent ... include creation of vast numbers of people fed from produce of fields on which they do not labour, tendencies toward intemperance, disease, restlessness, unemployment in downturns, and social instability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for evaluating the effects of commercialisation: if commerce is left without countervailing social/State measures, judge it harmful based on these social and demographic outcomes. Examples include factory laborers rendered intemperate and the danger that principals will 'shift for themselves' when enterprises fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population control rooted in moral and intellectual prerogatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The most efficient limit must be sought for in the moral and intellectual prerogatives of men, in their foresight, in their habituation to the comforts and decencies of society, in the pride of independence; but above all in the hope that enables [them] to withstand the tyranny of the present impulse, and in their expectation of honour or discredit from the rank, character, and condition of their children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author proposes normative evaluative criteria for population policy: rather than external legal or economic restraints, cultivate moral habits, education, and social incentives (hope, honour, pride of independence) to limit excessive population growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employers' social responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: It has not been made a part of the proposal, that the employers should be under any bond to counteract such injurious circumstances by education, discipline, or other efficient regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit criterion: employers ought to be bound (by law or obligation) to mitigate harmful effects of industrial employment (education, discipline, regulations). The absence of such obligations is presented as a failure to be remedied when judging industrial schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid large-scale dispossession of smallholders
rubrics_metrics.description: The moment the farmer obtains his wish he takes every particle of the land to himself, and re-lets the house to the labourer, who by this means is rendered miserable; the poor rate increased; the value of the estate to the landowner diminished; and the house suffered to go to decay ... formerly there were a great many cottagers who kept cows, but that the land is now thrown to the farmers ... in those parishes the poor rates have increased in an amazing degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as an evaluative test of agricultural policy and estate management: consolidation that displaces smallholders leads to measurable social harms (increased poor rates, poor health, revolutionary sentiment) and thus is judged negatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial principle: gradual, collective, and moral reform
rubrics_metrics.description: An evil which has come on gradually ... cannot be removed otherwise than gradually, and by the joint efforts of all. If we are a Christian nation, we must learn to act nationally, as well as individually, as Christians. ... more good would be done ... by the abolition of the lotteries, accompanied with a public and parliamentary declaration of the moral and religious grounds that had determined the legislature to this act; of their humble confidence in the blessing of God on the measure; and of their hope that this sacrifice in principle ... would be the more effective in restoring confidence between man and man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for evaluating reforms: prefer gradual, collective measures tied to moral/political legitimation (public declarations, religious/moral rationale) rather than sudden financial retrenchments which may worsen hardship. The author treats such moral pledges as more effective than mere fiscal measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation and education by leading classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Our manufacturers must consent to regulations; our gentry must concern themselves in the education as well as in the instruction of their natural clients and dependents — must regard their estates as offices of trust with duties to be performed, in the sight of God and their country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a standard for judging social improvement: elites (manufacturers and gentry) are to accept regulatory limits and active roles in education and stewardship; measuring success by whether they treat estates and industrial relations as moral trusts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual civic and charitable duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Let every man measure his efforts by his power and his sphere of action, and do all he can do! Let him contribute money where he cannot act personally; but let him act personally and in detail wherever it is practicable. Let us palliate where we cannot cure, comfort where we cannot relieve; and for the rest rely upon the promise of the King of kings ... 'Blessed are ye that sow beside all waters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline for individual behaviour and moral judgement: citizens should combine personal action with financial contribution, provide consolation when cure is impossible, and act within their means—presented as a standard for responsible civic conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bohn's Libraries editorial and selection standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The imprint of Bohn's Standard Library is a guaranty of good editing. This new and attractive form in which the volumes of Bohn's Standard Library are being issued is not meant to hide either indifference in the selection of books included in this well-known series, or carelessness in the editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher's evaluative claims about the series: criteria for inclusion and presentation are careful selection and good editing; volumes are 'small, handy, and complete.' Use as a standard for judging reprints/editions: editorial quality and careful selection are paramount.
